cells.tense: The hands that hold a thing level are here, with the pen, right now.
cells.act: hold space for what someone feels without fixing it
cells.ask: When a hard thing is handed to you, stay with it ten minutes and fix nothing. Notice what the staying asks of you, and what it gives.
cells.core:
Where people and structure meet, you know how to hold what someone's carrying without needing it solved tonight, and the things you've built keep standing after you step away. That steadiness is real, and it doesn't depend on a crisis. What's shifting now is something that wasn't true to begin with. A false premise gives way under its own weight, and nobody has to push it.

Before the next shift, hold one thing level while somebody feels what they feel. Don't steer it toward a point. Stay with them ten minutes without fixing, and let what's true keep itself a while.
cells.sheetLine: What you hold level doesn't need you to hold it harder.
cells.verb: holding weight until the structure is true
cells.place: in the last hour before a false structure comes down

cells.tense: The bracing has already started, and nothing here has come down yet.
cells.act: make the fair call about a feeling, yourself
cells.ask: Before you move to hold the next thing steady, write one line about what you're actually keeping in place. Then wait a day.
cells.core:
A decision is already made about how this will land, before anything has happened. The hands are braced, holding the walls by will — reinforcement nobody asked for, more structure than the thing needs. From outside it looks strong. From inside it costs: being the one who holds everything lead-proof is a job no one assigned, and a false thing kept in place by force puts off the clearing and doubles the weight.

At rest, this holds without crushing — weight carried, not gripped. So before you move to hold the next thing steady, write one line about what you're actually keeping in place, and give it a day. You'll know more about what's load-bearing once the walls settle.
cells.sheetLine: You're holding a wall before anything has moved.
cells.verb: holding weight until the structure is true
cells.place: in the last hour before a false structure comes down

cells.tense: The crown of the wall is gone, and it went while you were still standing at the door.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what is not
cells.ask: Name a thing that already fell this year and set it down, once, quietly to yourself. Then take a small step toward what isn't finished.
cells.core:
The clearing came somewhere in this part of life — something false came down quickly and truthfully, and some of it deserved to go. But the hands have stayed at the last door, holding up what's already gone, so the standing part hasn't properly started. It can look steady from outside, and inside it stalls: half the weight is going to an empty wall.

Balance here means holding without forcing. Before you take on the next thing, name one that is genuinely over and set its weight down, a single time, quietly to yourself, and then take one small step toward what's still unfinished. The step can be tiny. The clearing is already behind you.
cells.sheetLine: Some of the wall is down. Your hands are still at it.
cells.verb: holding weight until the structure is true
cells.place: in the last hour before a false structure comes down

cells.tense: The pen has been moving here, and the name signed to it isn't the one doing the work.
cells.act: start something for the spark of starting
cells.ask: Begin a thing with no plan for where it goes — a page, a repair, a question to someone who'd know — only because starting feels good.
cells.core:
When a false thing comes down quickly here, there's someone already watching who reads what's really load-bearing — by looking, not deciding. That reading keeps happening, unnoticed and uncounted, and the person carrying the story of it says they only got lucky. The story of luck is the thing to put down.

When a false structure clears, what couldn't hold goes, and something true keeps its place after, and the one holding it is you. So begin a thing for no reason but the start of it — a page, a repair, a question to someone who'd know. Nothing has to come of it, and you don't have to be ready.
cells.sheetLine: You keep saying it was luck. Nothing here was luck.
cells.verb: holding weight until the structure is true

attempts.check: The unsupported claim: that the person has built anything enduring in the part of life where this lands — Too Little in particular may be read as a history of building and losing, which the record does not say. A reader could reasonably say 'I never got to finish anything, so there's nothing here to release.' The asks survive that: each is one small move announced ahead of the event, not a verdict on what the person has done. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'steady hands' — I cut it from Too Little because it praises a quality I invented for them. The seat, Breakthrough, is where this looks least true: a false ceiling in the room, not a person's whole life.
